JSON: Name: der_spiegel_gaza_semiotics Title: Multimodal semiotic analysis of Der Spiegel magazine covers to quantify framing bias in coverage of the October 2023 Israeli war on Gaza Short Hypothesis: Presence of Holocaust-evocative visual or linguistic signs on Der Spiegel covers causes a lower rate of explicit mentions and condemnations of Israeli violations in the magazine's textual coverage of the October 2023 Gaza conflict. Related Work: Prior work divides into qualitative semiotic readings of press imagery (Barthes-style) and quantitative content/framing studies. Semiotic studies establish layered denotative/connotative readings but remain small-sample and interpretive, limiting reproducibility. Press-photograph analytic frameworks propose narrative and iconographic taxonomies for cover analysis, yet they are primarily manual and lack operationalized, numeric bias measures. Comparative magazine-cover case studies demonstrate interpretive depth but do not quantify causal links between visual signs and textual framing. Computational multimodal research on news framing has produced text classifiers and image detectors, but most systems treat modalities separately or fuse them heuristically and are rarely validated against semiotic expert coding. Limitations across these approaches include small or non-representative samples, low inter-annotator reliability for connotative categories, absence of standardized framing/bias metrics for imagery, weak causal identification strategies, and limited cross-outlet or cross-cultural validation. Abstract: This project addresses whether cover-level semiotic choices correlate with and influence textual framing of the October 2023 Israeli war on Gaza in Der Spiegel. We propose a multimodal pipeline that operationalizes semiotic signs (visual motifs and Holocaust-referential language) as discrete features, links them to article-level framing outcomes, and tests causal association using comparative and ablation experiments. The main contribution is a reproducible schema that combines expert semiotic coding, automated visual-symbol detectors, and transformer-based text framing classifiers to produce quantitative framing-bias measures for magazine covers. Expected outcomes are (1) an annotated dataset of cover images and articles, (2) validated multimodal models that predict explicit mention/condemnation rates, and (3) statistical estimates of the association between specific semiotic signs and textual framing. The impact is a method for converting interpretive semiotic claims into testable, multimodal metrics usable for cross-outlet comparison and automated monitoring of editorial framing. Experiments: Datasets: (A) Primary: Der Spiegel cover images and full article text for six issues dated 14/10/2023–20/04/2024 (n=6 cover-article pairs). (B) Extended comparative corpus: German national outlets (Die Zeit, Süddeutsche Zeitung, Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung, Bild, Der Tagesspiegel, Spiegel) cover images and lead articles about Gaza/Israel from 07/10/2023 to 30/04/2024, target N=250 cover-article pairs; images (JPEG/PNG), text OCR/HTML. Annotation: two trained annotators label (i) presence/absence of Holocaust-evocative visual signs (binary), (ii) Holocaust-referential language (binary), (iii) explicit mention of Israeli violations (binary), (iv) condemnation intensity (ordinal 0-3), and (v) dominant frame category (e.g., terrorism, humanitarian, historical justification). Resolve disagreements via adjudicator; report Cohen's kappa. Baselines: (1) human expert semiotic coding (gold), (2) text-only frame classifier (Transformer encoder fine-tuned for frame labels), (3) image-only classifier (ResNet/CNN fine-tuned to detect symbolic motifs), (4) simple heuristic lexical detector (holocaust lexicon). Proposed model: multimodal fusion (visual CNN embeddings + text Transformer, concatenated and passed to feed-forward classifier). Evaluation metrics: F1, precision, recall for detection tasks; Cohen's kappa for annotations; proportion and chi-square tests for mention/condemnation differences; logistic regression coefficients and odds ratios for association tests; effect sizes (Cohen's d) for continuous/ordinal outcomes; 95% confidence intervals. Experimental setup: split extended corpus into train/validation/test (70/15/15) stratified by outlet and date; perform 5-fold cross-validation for robustness. Ablations: (A) multimodal vs text-only; (B) multimodal vs image-only; (C) remove Holocaust-lexicon features from text; (D) remove visual symbolic channels from fusion. Statistical tests: compare proportions (chi-square) and model coefficients (Wald tests); report p-values and corrected p-values for multiple comparisons (Benjamini-Hochberg). Additional comparison: replicate analysis on a matched sample of international outlets (BBC, CNN) for external baseline if available. Risk Factors and Limitations: Small primary-sample size (six Der Spiegel covers) limits within-outlet causal power; extended corpus may still not fully represent editorial practices. Annotation subjectivity for connotative signs and Holocaust-evocative imagery may yield low inter-annotator reliability. Image classifiers may misinterpret symbolism (false positives/negatives) and fail on stylized or collage covers. OCR and HTML extraction errors can corrupt textual features. Confounding variables (issue editorial policies, headline placement, historical anniversaries) may bias associations and preclude causal attribution. Cross-outlet language and cultural differences limit generalization outside German media. Training deep multimodal models on limited labeled data risks overfitting and requires compute resources; results depend on pretraining and hyperparameter choices. Ethical risk: automated labeling of sensitive content (Holocaust references) can misclassify and amplify harm; dataset publication may require redaction. Statistical tests may detect associations but cannot conclusively prove editorial intent or causation.
